---
title: "Day 3 — Visualization"
subtitle: "Week 2 · ggplot2's grammar vs matplotlib's imperative style; the 5 charts that matter"
---

## Cheat sheet (60 seconds)

| Chart | R (ggplot2) | Python (matplotlib) |
|---|---|---|
| scatter | `geom_point()` | `ax.scatter(x, y)` |
| line | `geom_line()` | `ax.plot(x, y)` |
| histogram | `geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)` | `ax.hist(x, bins=20)` |
| box by group | `geom_boxplot(aes(x, y))` | `ax.boxplot([g1, g2, g3])` |
| bar | `geom_col()` (counted) / `geom_bar()` (auto) | `ax.bar(labels, heights)` |
| smooth/fit | `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` | `np.polyfit` + `ax.plot` |
| color by group | `aes(color = grp)` | loop + one `ax.scatter` per group |
| facets | `facet_wrap(~grp)` | `plt.subplots(nrows, ncols)` |
| labels | `labs(x =, y =, title =)` | `ax.set_xlabel(...)` etc |
| flip coords | `coord_flip()` | swap axes / `ax.barh` |
| save | `ggsave("p.png", plot, dpi = 300)` | `fig.savefig("p.png", dpi=300)` |

## Two philosophies, same picture

**ggplot2 is declarative**: you *declare* what maps to what — data, aesthetic
mappings, geometry — and the renderer decides pixels. **matplotlib is
imperative**: you *command* the canvas, step by step. The grammar scales to
facets and layers with zero extra code; the imperative style scales to
anything, eventually, with loops. Know both, default to the grammar when the
figure is "data says what".

```{webr}
#| label: grammar-r
library(tidyverse)

genes <- tibble(
  log2fc  = c(2.1, -1.8, 0.5, 3.0, 0.1, -0.4, 1.2, -2.2, 0.8, 2.5),
  logp    = c(6.1, 5.2, 0.4, 7.0, 0.1, 0.9, 2.2, 4.8, 1.1, 5.9),
  sig     = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
)

ggplot(genes, aes(x = log2fc, y = logp, color = sig)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change", y = "-log10 p",
       title = "Volcano plot", color = "padj < 0.05")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: grammar-py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

log2fc = [2.1, -1.8, 0.5, 3.0, 0.1, -0.4, 1.2, -2.2, 0.8, 2.5]
logp   = [6.1, 5.2, 0.4, 7.0, 0.1, 0.9, 2.2, 4.8, 1.1, 5.9]
sig    = [True, True, False, True, False, False, False, True, False, True]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for flag, style in [(True, "tab:red"), (False, "tab:gray")]:
    xs = [x for x, s in zip(log2fc, sig) if s == flag]
    ys = [y for y, s in zip(logp, sig)   if s == flag]
    ax.scatter(xs, ys, c=style, s=60, alpha=0.8, label=f"padj<0.05={flag}")
ax.axhline(-__import__("math").log10(0.05), ls="--", c="k", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="log2 fold change", ylabel="-log10 p", title="Volcano plot")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

Same volcano. Count the steps: the R version says *what* (map `sig` to
color, add a line at the threshold) and stops. The Python version has the
group-loop and the label bookkeeping spelled out — that code has to exist
somewhere, and ggplot's price is that you think in **mappings** instead.

## Mapping vs setting — the #1 ggplot mistake

```{webr}
#| label: mapping-r
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(x = 1:5, y = c(2, 3, 5, 4, 7), grp = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "B"))

# WRONG (but legal): colors every point red — "red" is a setting
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = "red")) + geom_point()

# RIGHT: color VARIES with grp — a mapping
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = grp)) + geom_point()

# RIGHT differently: setting a constant, outside aes()
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(color = "red")
```

Rule: **inside `aes()` = "this column drives it"; outside `aes()` = "make it
so"**. If a legend appears when you wanted a constant — you mapped by
accident. (matplotlib has no such trap; everything is a setting.)

## The 5 charts that matter

Ninety-five percent of bioinformatics reporting is these five. Learn the
decision rule, then the syntax.

### 1. Scatter — relationship between two continuous variables
(You just saw it: the volcano is a scatter.)

### 2. Line — a trend over an ordered variable

```{webr}
#| label: line-r
library(tidyverse)
growth <- tibble(
  hour   = rep(0:4, 2),
  od     = c(0.05, 0.12, 0.30, 0.72, 1.40, 0.05, 0.09, 0.15, 0.22, 0.30),
  strain = rep(c("WT", "mutant"), each = 5)
)

ggplot(growth, aes(hour, od, color = strain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "hours", y = "OD600")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: line-py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
hours  = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
wt     = [0.05, 0.12, 0.30, 0.72, 1.40]
mutant = [0.05, 0.09, 0.15, 0.22, 0.30]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(hours, wt, "o-", label="WT")
ax.plot(hours, mutant, "o-", label="mutant")
ax.set(xlabel="hours", ylabel="OD600")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

### 3. Histogram — the shape of one distribution

```{webr}
#| label: hist-r
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(42)
conc <- round(rlnorm(300, meanlog = log(25), sdlog = 0.6), 2)

ggplot(NULL, aes(conc)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "concentration (ng/uL)", y = "count",
       title = "Right-skewed — we'll meet this on Day 5")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: hist-py
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
conc = np.round(rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(25), sigma=0.6, size=300), 2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(conc, bins=np.arange(0, 160, 10), edgecolor="white")
ax.set(xlabel="concentration (ng/uL)", ylabel="count",
       title="Right-skewed — we'll meet this on Day 5")
plt.show()
```

Both seeded identically in spirit — `set.seed(42)` ↔
`np.random.default_rng(42)`. Different draws, same shape; the Day 5
reproducibility thread starts here.

### 4. Box (or violin) — one distribution, split by a group

```{webr}
#| label: box-r
library(tidyverse)
assay <- tibble(
  treatment = rep(c("control", "treated"), each = 6),
  conc = c(9, 11, 12, 10, 14, 13, 18, 21, 17, 22, 19, 20)
)

ggplot(assay, aes(treatment, conc, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "concentration (ng/uL)")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: box-py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
control = [9, 11, 12, 10, 14, 13]
treated = [18, 21, 17, 22, 19, 20]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.boxplot([control, treated])
ax.set_xticks([1, 2])
ax.set_xticklabels(["control", "treated"])
ax.set(ylabel="concentration (ng/uL)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The matplotlib boxplot quirk
`ax.boxplot` takes a **list of arrays**, one per group — no long data frame.
This is the moment most pandas users reach for seaborn
(`sns.boxplot(data=df, x="treatment", y="conc")`), which accepts tidy data
like ggplot. seaborn is one `#| packages: [seaborn]` away in these cells —
try it:

```{pyodide}
#| label: seaborn-demo
#| packages: [seaborn]
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
assay = __import__("pandas").DataFrame({
  "treatment": ["control"]*6 + ["treated"]*6,
  "conc": [9, 11, 12, 10, 14, 13, 18, 21, 17, 22, 19, 20]})

sns.boxplot(data=assay, x="treatment", y="conc", hue="treatment", legend=False)
plt.show()
```
(First run downloads the package — takes a few seconds; needs network.)
:::

### 5. Bar — comparing counts or summary values

```{webr}
#| label: bar-r
library(tidyverse)
reads <- tibble(sample = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
                millions = c(21.0, 4.2, 18.9))

ggplot(reads, aes(sample, millions)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "reads (millions)")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: bar-py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
samples  = ["S1", "S2", "S3"]
millions = [21.0, 4.2, 18.9]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.barh(samples, millions, color="steelblue")
ax.set(xlabel="reads (millions)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `geom_col` vs `geom_bar`, `bar` vs `hist`
R: `geom_bar()` counts rows for you; `geom_col()` plots values you already
have. Python: `ax.bar()` plots your heights; `ax.hist()` bins raw data.
Passing pre-counted data to a counting function (or vice versa) silently
squares your bars. Also: **bar charts start at 0** (length encodes value);
*never* use bars for means ± p-values from a baseline far from zero — points
or boxes instead.
:::

## Small multiples: facets ↔ subplots

```{webr}
#| label: facet-r
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)
peptides <- tibble(
  conc = c(rnorm(100, 30, 8), rnorm(100, 20, 6), rnorm(100, 25, 7)),
  peptide = rep(c("SubP", "Vaso", "Brady"), each = 100)
)

ggplot(peptides, aes(conc)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ peptide, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "concentration", y = "count")
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: facet-py
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
groups = {"SubP": rng.normal(30, 8, 100),
          "Vaso": rng.normal(20, 6, 100),
          "Brady": rng.normal(25, 7, 100)}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, sharey=True, figsize=(9, 3))
for ax, (name, vals) in zip(axes, groups.items()):
    ax.hist(vals, bins=12, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white")
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel="conc")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
plt.show()
```

One line of R per extra panel (`facet_wrap` re-tiles for any group count);
matplotlib's loop is fine but the axes bookkeeping is yours. This is the
grammar's superpower: **the figure structure is derived from the data, not
hand-built.**

## Making plots honest (both dialects)

::: {.callout-important}
## The 6-point pre-flight for every report figure
1. **Axis labels with units** — "conc (ng/uL)", not "conc"
2. **Title says the finding**, not the variable names
3. **Bins/widths chosen**, not defaulted (`binwidth`, `bins=`)
4. **N shown** somewhere — caption or facet title
5. **Colorblind-safe defaults** — the defaults above are; custom palettes check yours
6. **One message per plot** — if you need three legends, it's three plots
:::

Saving for the report: `ggsave("fig1.png", p, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)`
↔ `fig.savefig("fig1.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")` — always *before*
you close/quit the device (`plt.show()` clears nothing, R Studio does — a
classic blank-PNG mystery).

## Where in-browser plotting stands

| Works live on iPad | Doesn't (yet) |
|---|---|
| ggplot2 in `{webr}` cells ✓ | plotly interactivity |
| base R `plot()` ✓ | complex patched layouts |
| matplotlib in `{pyodide}` cells ✓ | plotnine (micropip only, slow install) |
| seaborn via micropip ✓ | — |

plotnine is literally ggplot syntax in Python
(`(ggplot(df, aes("x", "y")) + geom_point())`) — handy as a bridge, but it
installs on demand and is heavy; for the course, matplotlib fluency + the
grammar *vocabulary* is the durable combo.

## Drills (live pad)

```{webr}
#| label: drills
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(x = 1:20, y = (1:20)^2, grp = rep(c("A", "B"), 10))

# 1. Scatter of x vs y — then color it by grp. Which version creates a legend?

# 2. Line plot of x vs y — what does it look like? Why is a line the WRONG
#    geom for this data?

# 3. Histogram of y with binwidth 20

# 4. Boxplot of y split by grp

# 5. Bar plot of mean(y) per grp (hint: compute first, then geom_col)

# 6. Same scatter as 1 but with facets instead of colors

# 7. Add a smoothed trend to scatter 1: geom_smooth() — what method by default?

# 8. Make plot 1 publishable: labels + title in one chain
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. `aes(color = grp)` (mapping) makes the legend; `color = "red"` (setting) doesn't
2. A jagged zig-zag — lines imply ordered continuity; x here is categorical-ish identity
3. `ggplot(df, aes(y)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 20)`
4. `ggplot(df, aes(grp, y)) + geom_boxplot()`
5. `df |> group_by(grp) |> summarise(m = mean(y)) |>
   ggplot(aes(grp, m)) + geom_col()`
6. `+ facet_wrap(~grp)` — same data, side-by-side panels
7. loess by default under n = 1000 (`method = "lm"` for a straight fit)
8. `+ labs(x = "...", y = "...", title = "...")`
:::

## Python drills (live pad)

```{pyodide}
#| label: drills-py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
x = np.arange(1, 21)
y = x ** 2
grp = np.array(list("AB") * 10)

# 1. fig, ax = plt.subplots() — scatter colored by grp (two .scatter calls
#    or one with c=grp) — which approach gives a legend for free?

# 2. ax.plot(x, y) — same zig-zag problem as R?

# 3. ax.hist(y, bins=...)

# 4. ax.boxplot([y[grp == "A"], y[grp == "B"]])

# 5. Bar of mean(y) per group — compute, then ax.bar

# 6. Two subplots side by side (1 row, 2 cols), one histogram per group —
#    notice the manual loop ggplot's facet_wrap replaces

# 7. Save your favorite: fig.savefig(...) — check the file exists in the
#    virtual FS: import os; os.listdir(".")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers (Python)
1. Two calls with `label=` then `ax.legend()` — matplotlib never auto-legends
2. Yes — geometry advice is language-independent
4. `ax.set_xticks([1, 2]); ax.set_xticklabels(["A", "B"])` to name the boxes
5. `means = [y[grp == g].mean() for g in "AB"]` then `ax.bar(["A", "B"], means)`
6. `fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2); for ax, g in zip(axes, "AB"): ax.hist(y[grp == g])`
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — fix the mapped accident

This plot shows a legend nobody wants. Fix it so points are steelblue,
constant.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-mapping
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(x = 1:10, y = (1:10) + rnorm(10))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = "steelblue")) +
  geom_point(size = 3)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-mapping"}
Move the color out of `aes()` — into `geom_point()`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-mapping"}
```r
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue")
```
:::

### Exercise 2 — from long data to faceted histograms

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-facet
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(7)
long <- tibble(
  conc    = c(rnorm(80, 30, 5), rnorm(80, 22, 5), rnorm(80, 26, 5)),
  peptide = rep(c("SubP", "Vaso", "Brady"), each = 80)
)

# one histogram per peptide, sharing the x scale, 3 rows
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-facet"}
`facet_wrap(~ peptide, ncol = 1)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-facet"}
```r
ggplot(long, aes(conc)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ peptide, ncol = 1)
# shared scales are the default (fixed); scales = "free" would UN-share them
```
:::

### Exercise 3 — the Python twin

Same data, one figure, 3 stacked subplots, shared x-range:

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d3-facet-py
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
groups = {"SubP": rng.normal(30, 5, 80),
          "Vaso": rng.normal(22, 5, 80),
          "Brady": rng.normal(26, 5, 80)}

______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-facet-py"}
`plt.subplots(3, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(6, 7))` then loop `zip`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-facet-py"}
```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(6, 7))
for ax, (name, vals) in zip(axes, groups.items()):
    ax.hist(vals, bins=12, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white")
    ax.set(title=name)
plt.show()
```
:::

### Exercise 4 — scatter with a fitted line, both dialects

Add a linear fit to the scatter of `hours` vs `od`. R gets `geom_smooth` for
free — Python needs two lines of `polyfit`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-smooth
library(tidyverse)
od <- tibble(hour = 0:4,
             od   = c(0.05, 0.12, 0.30, 0.72, 1.40))

ggplot(od, aes(hour, od)) +
  geom_point() +
  ______     # add the linear smooth with its confidence band
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-smooth"}
`geom_smooth(method = "lm")`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-smooth"}
```r
ggplot(od, aes(hour, od)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
# exponential-looking growth — a straight line underfits; try
# geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ log(x)) and compare
```
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d3-smooth-py
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
hours = np.arange(0, 5)
od    = np.array([0.05, 0.12, 0.30, 0.72, 1.40])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(hours, od)
# fit a line: slope, intercept = np.polyfit(hours, od, 1), then plot it
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-smooth-py"}
`np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` returns `[slope, intercept]`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-smooth-py"}
```python
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(hours, od, 1)
ax.plot(hours, slope * hours + intercept, "r--")
ax.set(xlabel="hour", ylabel="OD600")
plt.show()
```
:::

### Exercise 5 — the publishable rescue

This plot has four problems from the pre-flight list. Name them, then fix
them (R; the fixes transfer 1:1).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-rescue
library(tidyverse)
dat <- tibble(
  group = rep(c("ctrl", "low", "high"), each = 30),
  val   = c(rnorm(30, 10), rnorm(30, 11), rnorm(30, 12))
)

ggplot(dat, aes(group, val)) +
  geom_point()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-rescue"}
No labels; meaningless point cloud where a summary would do; group order is
alphabetical not meaningful; no sense of n.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-rescue"}
```r
ggplot(dat, aes(factor(group, c("ctrl", "low", "high")), val)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90", outlier.alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "dose group", y = "value (units)",
       title = "Value increases with dose",
       subtitle = paste0("n = ", nrow(dat), ", 10 per group"))
# fixes: ordered x, box shows distribution, real labels, n in subtitle
```
:::

## Common pitfalls (real ones)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. The default-plot trap in loops
Building figures inside a `for` loop without `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` (or
R's `print(p)` inside loops/functions) produces either 30 overlapping
figures or blank output. R: ggplots **must be printed** in loops/functions —
auto-printing is a top-level-only kindness. Python: create axes explicitly,
always.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. Histogram bin-count lies
The same data with `bins=5` vs `bins=50` tells opposite stories. Never
publish a default histogram; pick `binwidth` from the data's scale and say
so in the caption.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. Dual y-axes
Seems efficient, secretly partisan: each axis is scaled independently, so
you choose the crossing point. If two series need one canvas, facet or
normalize — don't dual-axis.
:::

## Self-quiz — predict the output

```{webr}
#| label: quiz
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4), y = c(2, 4, 5, 9), g = c("a", "a", "b", "b"))

# Q1: how many points, and what colors?
ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = g)) + geom_point()

# Q2: how many points, and what colors?
ggplot(df, aes(x, y), color = "blue") + geom_point()

# Q3: what does this render — points, line, or both?
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + geom_line()

# Q4: how many panels?
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~g)

# Q5: does this error?
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_histogram()
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quiz answers
1. 4 points, 2 colors + a legend — mapped
2. 4 blue points, no legend — set... actually: setting outside `aes()` at
   the plot level does nothing to geoms here; points render with the default
   color and no legend. The fix is `geom_point(color = "blue")`
3. Both — geoms stack; order = drawing order
4. 2 — one per level of g
5. No — it runs and bins `y` (the only aesthetic); a warningless histogram
   of the wrong variable is worse than an error. Read your x-axis.
:::
